blocks.content: This final module of the course turns to networking specifically as it applies to real system design, the practical infrastructure choices behind large, real world applications. A CDN, content delivery network, is one of the most common, foundational pieces of that infrastructure, and this opening topic explains exactly what problem it solves and how.

If you have ever streamed a video or loaded a website that felt genuinely fast regardless of where in the world you actually were, a CDN was almost certainly working invisibly behind the scenes to make that happen.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437874087-722863610.png
1. The Real Problem: Physical Distance Genuinely Costs Time
blocks.text: 1. The Real Problem: Physical Distance Genuinely Costs Time

blocks.content: A single origin server sits in one physical location. A user genuinely far away from that location, on the other side of the world, has every single request travel a real, long physical distance, and that distance directly translates into real, noticeable latency, no matter how fast the server itself actually is.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437874087-749141919.png
blocks.alt: The Real Problem: Physical Distance Genuinely Costs Time

blocks.content: 2. The Fix: Spreading Copies Across Edge Servers
blocks.text: 2. The Fix: Spreading Copies Across Edge Servers

blocks.content: A CDN solves this by copying content out from the origin server to many edge servers, physically distributed across different regions around the world. Instead of every single user request traveling all the way back to one distant origin, it can instead be served from whichever edge server happens to be physically closest to that specific user.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437874087-132239837.png
blocks.alt: The Fix: Spreading Copies Across Edge Servers

blocks.content: 3. Serving From the Nearest Location

When a user request actually arrives, the CDN routes it to the nearest available edge server, not all the way back to the original distant origin. Because the physical distance involved is now dramatically shorter, the response genuinely arrives much faster, for users everywhere, not just those who happen to live near the origin.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437874087-389519571.png
4. What Actually Gets Cached at the Edge
blocks.text: 4. What Actually Gets Cached at the Edge

blocks.content: Static content, images, videos, scripts, stylesheets, content that stays genuinely the same for every user, is ideally suited to being cached and served directly from the edge. Highly personalized or constantly changing content is less naturally suited to simple edge caching, since a cached copy could quickly become stale or simply wrong for a specific user.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437874087-77058115.png
blocks.alt: What Actually Gets Cached at the Edge

blocks.content: {"headers":["Content type","Well suited to CDN caching"],"rows":[["Images, videos, scripts, stylesheets","Yes, genuinely ideal"],["Highly personalized, per user content","Less naturally suited, needs more careful handling"]]}
5. A Genuine Side Benefit: Protecting the Origin
blocks.text: 5. A Genuine Side Benefit: Protecting the Origin

blocks.content: Without a CDN, every single request, no matter how many users are actually asking for the exact same content, hits the origin server directly, a real risk of overload under genuinely heavy traffic. With a CDN, edge servers absorb the vast majority of requests for cacheable content, meaning the origin sees dramatically less direct load, a genuine, practical reliability benefit beyond just raw speed.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437874088-430508389.png
blocks.alt: A Genuine Side Benefit: Protecting the Origin

blocks.title: A benefit worth stating explicitly
blocks.content: A CDN is often thought of purely as a speed optimization, but this origin protection effect is just as real and just as valuable, especially during sudden, unexpected traffic spikes.
6. A Real World Analogy

A single central warehouse, far from most customers, versus local grocery stores stocked with copies of the popular items customers actually want, captures this well. Customers get what they need quickly from a nearby local store, rather than every single purchase requiring a trip all the way out to the one distant central warehouse.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437995011-3823488.png

blocks.title: This connects directly to the DNS module
blocks.content: A CDN commonly uses DNS itself, covered in full in the DNS module, to actually direct a specific user to the nearest edge server, often returning a different IP address depending on where in the world the request is actually coming from.
7. Real, Everyday CDN Use

Streaming video platforms rely heavily on CDNs to deliver video smoothly to viewers everywhere. Nearly every major website serves its images and static assets through a CDN. Software and game download distribution, needing to move large files to users worldwide efficiently, is another genuinely common, everyday CDN use case.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437995013-783116604.png

8. Common Mistakes and Key Takeaways

["Assuming a CDN is purely a speed optimization, when protecting the origin server from direct overload is just as real and valuable a benefit.","Assuming a CDN works equally well for all content types, when highly personalized, constantly changing content needs more careful handling than simple static asset caching.","A CDN spreads copies of content across geographically distributed edge servers, reducing the physical distance a request has to travel.","Static content is ideally suited to edge caching; highly personalized content needs more care.","A CDN also protects the origin server by absorbing the vast majority of requests at the edge."]
items: Assuming a CDN is purely a speed optimization, when protecting the origin server from direct overload is just as real and valuable a benefit.
Assuming a CDN works equally well for all content types, when highly personalized, constantly changing content needs more careful handling than simple static asset caching.
A CDN spreads copies of content across geographically distributed edge servers, reducing the physical distance a request has to travel.
Static content is ideally suited to edge caching; highly personalized content needs more care.
A CDN also protects the origin server by absorbing the vast majority of requests at the edge.
